For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring the council replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.

The decision was the county's. A county rule now requires reflective letters on every road it maintains, and every road in Hollins Ford is one of them. Within a week the ambulance crews wrote to ask that the new signs keep Marrow's letter shapes. On forty years of night calls, they said, his boards were the first in the county they could read from a moving cab, and drivers who mistook turnings in other towns found Hollins Ford's streets on the first pass.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, found his patterns rolled in the old workshop: a full alphabet traced on brown paper. She asked the county to swap its standard letters for Marrow's, and the foundry cast every new sign from his tracings, enlarged by a fifth because the post office wanted larger letters. The care in those patterns shows best at the Gates, two of the first boards he painted. He gave the U of Upper Gate a long tail and the L of Lower Gate a heavy foot, and in four decades the crews never once mixed up the two Gates, even at night. When a delivery van struck the Upper Gate post in May, the post snapped where it had rotted, and the board came away whole, its edges as crisp as the day he cut them.

At a town meeting in June, residents voted to hang the old boards on the town hall stairs. They spent a fortnight in storage at the depot shed and then went up in street order, one landing at a time.

Marrow's boards earned their place on those stairs. Every driver who reaches Hollins Ford after dark still finds the way by letters he drew on Tanner Street, and the foundry did well to copy them line for line.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun, and she had built both of them herself long ago, a summer's work. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way. Mrs. Pellow handed me a veil and mentioned that she wintered at her daughter's in Lisle.

Soon I could lift a frame without flinching. One hot morning in July the sound of the nearer hive rose to a roar, and a swarm streamed out over the lilac by the back gate while my mother stared from the clothesline by our back steps. I found it settled high under the eaves of the shed. Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof herself and brushed the bees into a box, and we set it under the pear tree by her kitchen as a third, smaller colony.

What I thought about most, though, was the lane. Every evening the Corder brothers practised on Tamsin Lane, and every pitch that got past the catcher skipped under the fence and fetched up against the hives. Each time I heard the smack of a ball against the boards, I pictured the throw that would one day split a box wide open.

In August we took away the full frames. She sold the honey on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. Every evening she had me repeat what to watch for: the weight of a box, the colour of the brood, the bees at the entrance at dusk. On the first of September she put her hive tool in my hands and caught the train to Lisle.

Now the nights are turning cold, and until April the three hives are in my care. The smaller colony from the eaves still feels light when I tip its box, and on windy nights I lie awake wondering whether it has stored enough honey to last until spring. When the snow melts, the Corder brothers will be back on the lane.

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead. Then the streetlights on the hill come on, and the first swifts drop into the chimney, each with a sharp bank to the left, while the last bus passes the school gates.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. Those notebooks are the reason the chimney is still standing.

The storm two winters ago split the chimney with a crack from its top to the roofline. The council proposed having it pulled down, since a proper repair would cost more than demolition. Reyburn went to the March meeting, he told me, only to ask whether the work could wait until the swifts had left, and he set his notebooks on the table because he had carried them in. The councillors read them through and voted to keep the chimney standing for the swifts.

The masons who mended it chose lime mortar matched to the old, knowing that cheap cement would crack the soft brick and dry too smooth for a swift's claws. A century after it was built, the chimney stands as straight and sound as the day its last brick was laid, the best-made thing on the hill.

Whoever laid that brick built well enough for a furnace and, a hundred years on, well enough for six thousand swifts. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand over the empty schoolyard until they return in May, as solid as it has always been.
